utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic. PRESIDING OFFICER: And if we could have the appearances, please, from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Presiding Officer, good morning counsel. Counsel for the Prosecution appear Ms. Marie Tuma, trial attorney, and I, Ekkehard Withopf, senior trial attorney. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. I'm sorry. I didn't actually get any interpretation of that. Did anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now? PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes. Thank you. And Sarajevo, can you hear us? Sarajevo, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you well. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Just before we start, we're here to take the evidence of the witness Mr. Vehbija Karic today, by way of deposition, pursuant to Rule 71 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. As such, I have been appointed as Presiding Officer by the Trial Chamber decision of the 11th of June, 2003. These proceedings are in open session and will be recorded with a full transcript, and will be transmitted to the Trial Chamber for eventual inclusion in the trial record. Any objections raised by a party during the deposition will be noted and submitted to the Trial Chamber for a decision. Before we start, a couple of practical points. First, the schedule. We have four half days available to us, and we will sit from 9.30 to 10.30 each day, break for 15 minutes, to 10.45, sit until 11.45, break for another 15 minutes, and then sit from 12.00 until 1.00 p.m. Of course, this is subject to change, if need be, especially in light of the witness's health. Mr. Withopf, first of all, how long do you anticipate taking for the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution anticipates today and tomorrow for the examination-in-chief. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Please, of course, bear in mind that we may need a short period of time for re-examination. Now, an issue that does seem to arise in connection with taking deposition evidence is how to address the Presiding Officer. It is perfectly acceptable to address me as Madam Presiding Officer or as Ms. Featherstone, whichever comes easier to you. I would note as well that the accused Sefer Halilovic, having been given the opportunity to attend these proceedings, has waived his right to be present by way of a letter dated the 17th of June, 2003. Now, Mr. Hodzic, the Trial Chamber has received your request filed yesterday to withdraw as counsel and has directed me to continue with the deposition evidence this week. Until that matter is resolved, you have the right to attend and to cross-examine the witness, pursuant to Rule 71(C) of the Rules. You're welcome to participate fully in the proceedings. If you choose not to, the Trial Chamber will, of course, be informed of that. Is there anything you would like to add at this moment, Mr. Hodzic? Please note: I'm not inviting you to argue your position; simply to let me know if perhaps you have changed your view or if there's anything more that should be on the record at this time along with the deposition evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Presiding Officer, I have nothing to add to what I've already written, so I stand by that for the time being. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Mr. Withopf, is there anything you would like to add? As I say, it's not the place to debate the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There's only one issue the Prosecution wishes to raise. Since Defence counsel in his yesterday's motion announced that he will not be in a position to actively participate in the deposition proceedings, the Prosecution wishes to state that it considers this as a waiver of the Defence rights under Rule 71 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. PRESIDING OFFICER: Very well. That will be noted by the Trial Chamber and they will, of course, have the final say on the matter. Right. Then I think we should begin with the evidence. Mr. Karic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. If you would please take the solemn declaration and the Court deputy with you will assist you, and then I will explain very briefly a couple of provisions of the Rules which relate to the procedure today. So if you could please stand to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Karic. Mr. Karic, these proceedings are in public and your evidence will form part of the public record of the trial of Sefer Halilovic. If there is any evidence or answer to a question which for some reason you do not want to state in open session, please say so and we can go into a short private session to discuss this. Secondly, I must inform you that pursuant to Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, you may object to answering any question that may incriminate you. In that case, I will bring your objection to the attention of the Trial Chamber at the first possible opportunity, so that, if may be, it can be resolved before the end of this deposition procedure. Finally, please do not hesitate to inform me or the court deputy who is with you if you're feeling ill or tired. In that case, we can take a short break, even if it is not the scheduled time, to allow you to recover. Now, you will first be asked questions by the Prosecution and then possibly by the Defence counsel. So, Mr. Withopf, would you like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, my name is Ekkehard Withopf, and I'm a trial attorney, and I'm acting on behalf of the Prosecution. Together with me is Ms. Marie Tuma. She is also a Prosecution trial attorney. Today and tomorrow, and probably on Thursday, we will put to you a number of questions. We ask you to very carefully listen to the questions and to answer them as short and precisely as possible. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, can you please inform us about your full name, your date of birth, and your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: My name is Vehbija Karic. I was born on the 21st of April, 1938, in Podgrade, the municipality of Pale, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I've retired a few years ago, so I've been a retiree now for those few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, from which position did you retire?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I was a brigadier of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And when did you retire? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 1st of June, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And has there been a particular reason why you retired at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some reasons. The Superior Command, the General Staff, asked for my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And why did your superior commander ask for your retirement?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, my superior officer did not ask for me to retire; I submitted a request in writing, because I wished to retire, after having completed over 40 years of service, and I felt exhausted, from the point of view of my health. A year or so after that, I did indeed retire, and I also fell ill. This led to surgery. I had a tumor on the stomach, and I was treated in hospital, and I've literally been struggling to survive ever since I had this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, thank you. What was your rank within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ABiH, when you retired?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I held the rank of brigadier. From the 12th of January, 1993, until my retirement, I was a brigadier of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And Mr. Karic, when did you join the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I joined on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And prior to having joined the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, have you been a member of any other army?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I was in the Yugoslav People's Army. I held the rank of colonel in the command of the 2nd Military District, and I worked for General Kukanjac, who was commander of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Karic, I'm now moving to a different subject-matter, and it concerns the Operation NERETVA-93. Are you familiar with the Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: A few days before the inspection team was set up, in the General Staff, they decided to establish an inspection team, and I was on that team. The team consisted of several men who were supposed to carry out an inspection of the units in the Neretva River Valley. These were the units of the 6th, 4th, and 3rd Corps respectively, because some weaknesses had been exhibited before that, and they needed to be viewed. Also, proposals were supposed to be made to the General Staff upon completion of this inspection as to how these weaknesses should be dealt with. Our task was also to coordinate, cooperation among the different corps, the 4th, the 6th, and the 3rd Corps, whose headquarters were in Zenica. With this team, we went to Herzegovina and we carried out this task, according to orders. We carried out the required inspections. Since we learned from the commander of the 4th Corps in Mostar, Commander Arif Pasalic, personally reported to us in Jablanica. He said that he had some information as to the HVO preparing to attack the left bank of the Neretva in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, may I interrupt you at this --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: And the Bosniak population in that area. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Other than examination of troops and coordination, was there any military purpose, was there any military aim of the Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: After this information that we received, and after our stay in Jablanica, and having received all this information, the military purpose was to help Mostar, in view of the preparations that were being carried out in order to launch an attack on the left bank of the Neretva River, Eastern Mostar, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would the assessment be correct that the military purpose was to deblockade Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, to an extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This team you are talking about, who was a member of this team?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: This team was headed by the chief of General Staff, Sefer Halilovic; then there was Rifat Bilajac, Zicro Suljevic, Vehbija Karic, Dzemal Najetovic and Namik Dzankovic. That was the team that had set out with this assignment, or rather, on orders of the General Staff and orders of Rasim Delic. This is the task I've already referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what role did you play in this team?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Like the other members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what were their functions, please?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Inspection, coordination, cooperation amongst units, and certainly exercising direct influence amongst the units in order to redress some of the weaknesses that had manifested themselves prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The team you are talking about, was it involved in combat operations? Was it involved in commanding and directing combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: We were not tasked with commanding units. Rasim Delic, chief of the General Staff, did not issue such orders to us. Our role was one of inspection and coordination. And in the Operation Neretva that followed later, we coordinated and channeled these activities in accordance with the authority vested in us by the commander. He visited us and he signed combat documents in Jablanica. During the few days that were devoted to preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Operation NERETVA-93, where and when has it been planned?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was planned by the General Staff, and on the basis of information received from subordinate commanders and commands, and in accordance with the necessity involved. The operations department of the General Staff was involved, as well as the corps commands. This was planned in the stage when we were leaving Sarajevo, going to Jablanica, having received all this information about this imminent danger. So we were supposed to help Mostar and the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there a meeting prior to your leaving to the area that set up the framework of this operation?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Several times during the days that preceded our departure, we had meetings at the General Staff. A current issue was helping the 4th Corps on the basis of information that was coming in daily in terms of the HVO preparing to attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I interrupt --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: -- the east part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I interrupt you at this point. Has there been a meeting prior to your leaving the area, a few months prior to the commencement of the operation?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: No. For a few months, no. This was a current issue, say 10 or 15 days at the most, prior to our departure from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there a meeting in Zenica dealing with the Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: There was a meeting in Zenica, but it was a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to what extent --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: And in the presence of all the corps commanders, the commander of the 5th Corps wasn't in a position to come to that meeting. The minister of the MUP was there, Bakir Alispahic. The meeting lasted for two or three days in Zenica. It was a briefing. And at that meeting we discussed the results of combat activities to date, the weaknesses, and we discussed what we should undertake in the forthcoming period in order to improve the effectiveness of our forces, of our units. At that meeting, it was said that because of the possibility of a threat to the 4th Corps in Mostar, it was necessary to help that corps. But there was no detailed military planning in Zenica. There was only a general conclusion, according to which it was necessary to support the 4th Corps, the General Staff of the BH army had to support the 4th Corps. That was the general conclusion that was reached at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there Sefer Halilovic -- did Mr. Sefer Halilovic also take part in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, Rasim Delic participated, as commander of the General Staff, Sefer Halilovic as the chief of the General Staff. Most of the corps commanders, with the exception of Dudakovic, most of the chiefs from the General Staff of the BH army, the Minister of the Interior, Bakir Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Alispahic. At the moment, I can't remember whether anyone else was present, but it was a meeting at which we wanted to discuss the combat activities of the army to date and to indicate what the weaknesses were and conclusions were reached as to what action should be taken in the future and how to eliminate certain weaknesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In relation to Operation NERETVA-93, was there any discussion about the command of this operation? First part of my question, and about which units should be involved in that operation, second part of my question.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I have my war diary with me. With your permission, I'll consult it to remind myself of that period. I don't think we went into details. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, before you respond --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This wasn't discussed in any detail at all. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, just a point, if I may, please. Mr. Withopf, has this document been provided to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I actually must say I'm not sure about, but it can be provided now. PRESIDING OFFICER: Okay. If you'd like to carry on with the questioning and then we'll deal with the question of whether it needs to be exhibited at the end of your line of questioning. Thank you. My apologies, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, if the need arises we will come back to this war diary, but at this point in time, we actually don't see the need for that. The question was, Mr. Karic: Has there been any discussion in Zenica in August 1993 which units should be involved in Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I'd like to point out that we didn't go into details at that meeting in Zenica with regard to the participation of units, but a general conclusion was reached that units of the 4th Corps should be included, units of the 4th Corps which were threatened by the HVO, the units of the 6th Corps from Korenica and up to Dreznica, and in order to support from the 3rd Corps in Zenica with the coordination of the General Staff. So there was a general discussion as to which units might be included, might be used to support the 4th Corps in Mostar. We didn't go into any other details. That is an issue that was addressed only subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In Zenica in August 1993, was there any discussion about using units from the 1st Corps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What does it mean, "in general terms"?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: That perhaps the 1st Corps, together with its forces, might be able to provide support, if such a conclusion was reached, a conclusion which was reached later and a battalion was engaged from the 1st Corps. In the course of the preparations for the Operation NERETVA-93. All I want to do is to confirm that at the meeting in Zenica, the discussion was of a general nature, and it was said that it was the General Staff's obligation to support, to help Mostar and the 4th Corps, but no specific orders were issued at that time. That is something that was done later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Moving on to the Operation NERETVA-93 and its preparation itself, were there any units involved from outside the area?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some units from the 6th Corps were involved, some units from the 3rd Corps, the entire 4th Corps, which was in the surroundings, in Mostar, which was surrounded in Mostar, and from Sarajevo, a battalion was brought in, from the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigades, and from the independent battalion. There were about 300 men in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You just mentioned the 9th and the 10th Brigades of the 2nd Independent Battalion. To which corps did such unit belong to?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: They belonged to the 1st Corps, the 1st Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The corps which was responsible for the defence of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 9th and 10th Brigades, who were the commanders of such units?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 9th Brigade was Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo, and the commander of the 10th was Musan Topalovic, also known as Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 9th and the 10th Brigades, in comparison with other military units, how would you describe their reputation?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: According to the information available at the time, through reports and contacts, while in Sarajevo, it mainly concerned brigades. It had also achieved certain combat results, but mostly consisted of men from the old town and the suburban parts of the old town. Some of them, a large number of -- then consisted of people who were of a criminal kind. They would abuse drugs and so on. And they were involved in certain events, from 1992 up until that period, 1993. They exhibited a certain degree of willfulness, a lack of discipline, and men who had no military education led those units. They were criminal personalities themselves. I'm thinking of Ramiz Delalic, Celo and Musan Topalovic, Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's first talk about Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and Musan Topalovic, Caco. You're referring to their criminal background. Can you please provide us some more details in that respect?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As far as Ramiz Delalic, Celo is concerned, at the very beginning he was involved in a murder a few days before the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina commenced in Bascarsija, in the old town. He lived in Sarajevo up until then and was well known to the Ministry of the Interior organs, known for his violent and criminal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You're mentioning one murder in 1992. Who was the victim of this murder?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: If I have heard you correctly, this happened over a few days at the beginning of April. The Serbian people attending a wedding went towards an orthodox church in Bascarsija and a conflict broke out in which Ramiz Delalic, Celo, shot someone at the wedding, someone in the column heading towards the church, shot him from a pistol. This resulted in a lot of animosity on the part of many there, and spread an atmosphere of aggression among the public. Over that period that preceded the commencement of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This person who was killed, was it a civilian?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, a civilian. That person wasn't wearing a uniform. The person was an elderly person attending the wedding. In accordance with the tradition of weddings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were referring to --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you were referring to further crimes committed by Ramiz Delalic. Can you please go into further detail.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, the other crimes were more a matter of demonstrating a lack of military discipline once the war broke out. The selection of commanders wasn't official. It wasn't official by the Territorial Defence headquarters, which is what would be expected when former units in other countries. So you would expect such a selection to take place. In this case it was more spontaneous. The principle applied was kind of self-management. The soldiers themselves would select men with the support of other men who exerted influence in the old town at the time. Not coming to meetings, the commanders of the 1st Corps, identifying men, combatants in the town, the attack against the headquarters of the Supreme Command, et cetera. These are all matters that indicate arrogant behaviour, disorganised behaviour on the part of Ramiz Delalic, Celo, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you were stating that the Ministry of the Interior was well aware of Mr. Ramiz Delalic's criminal behaviour. Can you please explain how they got to know and what their reaction has been.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no particular reaction, because our resistance was more a matter of a spontaneous development, a result of the patriotism of the people who wanted to avoid being killed, as they had been killed in the course of the Second World War, when they waited at the Drina bridges Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for 24 hours and were then killed and thrown into the Drina River. Many people didn't want to suffer the same fate. They wanted to resist. And those days, patriotism was very much valued, value was placed on those who could join the resistance. So if Ramiz Delalic was selected by the combatants who formed his 9th Brigade, this was not that important. He was selected without the influence of the Territorial Defence staff, which was formed. This was accepted as such, and this is how people proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The fact that he was known as a murderer, did it cause any reaction from the official authorities in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, it didn't, because it was registered, but the events that unfolded after that event were such that -- the events were such that the small, the minor episodes that had happened before, not much importance was given to this, because there was a far greater danger. They had started shelling Sarajevo on the 5th and 6th of April, and this happened a few days before that. I want to say that the events that subsequently unfolded were far more dramatic, far more important as far as survival is concerned, far more important than an episode that happened a few days prior to that event. This was noted, but no particular importance was given to this event, as far as launching investigation, et cetera, is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on to Musan Topalovic, Caco. What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: A musician before the war, a man who also liked the easy life. He wasn't particularly educated. He was selected by the man as a commander, just like Celo was, and later on, when the unit was formed, he demonstrated various kinds of weaknesses: willfulness, disobedience, later on. We found out about certain murders. We found out about these murders towards the end of the war, or after he had been killed, in October 1993. Up until then, we didn't know about this; at least, I didn't know about this. He was prone to willfulness. He was undisciplined. And that is why a decision was finally taken to use military force to eliminate the negative characteristics of those units, for example, the 9th and 10th. And this was done by the Supreme Command and the General Staff, in October 1993, which is when Caco was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The negative characteristics, as you described, the characteristics of the 9th and 10th Brigades, what are these negative characteristics in more detail?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, up until the time that they were used in combat activity, and given what they had done in Grabovica, up until what they did in Grabovica, there was no animosity, not an official -- not officially speaking, although we knew that they did not follow -- they did not conduct themselves in a disciplined way and that they weren't completely integrated in a system of military subordination. We knew that they behaved in a quite arrogant manner and that the atmosphere in those units, especially if we're referring to the misappropriation of property in Sarajevo shops and supermarkets, department stores, and we knew that they would satisfy their own needs. We knew that such characteristics were present in these units and that they demonstrated criminal form of behaviour. These elements were present. And when they did what they did in Grabovica, it became clear that drugs were being used too and that there were individuals who were also capable of committing such crimes, such as the crimes committed in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You're saying the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades were satisfying their own needs. Would a description of such behaviour as robberies be the correct one?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was understood. Many citizens complained later on, after members from the 9th and 10th Brigade had been arrested, and after the event in October, when these units were being dealt with. Many citizens complained about the violent behaviour, about intrusion into their flats, about threats, requests for money or gold, requests that the citizens should give money or gold to these units. So much was found out when people felt that they could speak about these matters, because up until then they weren't able to do so, since they risked being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The risk to being killed, being killed by whom?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question? I didn't hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just saying, Mr. Karic, that people only came out afterwards what happened to them because they were fearing to be killed, and my question was: From whom -- or who did they think would kill them?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the men under Caco and Celo, the men who behaved in this criminal manner, and whenever they found out that some of the citizens had property of some kind, they would force them to hand this property over. There was no resistance in such cases, because armed men would enter flats. They would threat and they would take what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is there any background for believing that the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades would have killed such people if they would have offered resistance?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I know of one case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please detail this case.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Ibro Zulic, who was a relative of Dusan Topalovic, Caco, the uncle of Dusan Topalovic, Caco, and he worked for a humanitarian organisation called Sinovi Bosne the sons of Bosna. Caco found out that he had money. He ordered his men to bring him in. He beat him up, so badly that he almost lost his eyes. He threatened to use battery acid on him. He kept him there for two days, until he managed to get about 10.000 German marks from him, and then he released him in this beaten up state. I know about this case and this man, Ibro Zulic is still alive today. He lives in the old town in Sarajevo. And he was his uncle on his mother's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were also referring, Mr. Karic, that soldiers of the 9th and 10th Brigades were using drugs. Can you please detail this. What kind of drugs, how often, what has been the result of using drugs?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: During the war, we who lived in Sarajevo, that was under siege, witnessed the fact that drugs did indeed get into Sarajevo from the direction of Herzegovina. A series of people who were within the 9th and 10th Brigades were drug addicts before the war too, so they continued using drugs because drugs did get into Sarajevo. And they managed to get hold of drugs. Their behaviour was unpredictable, so this was a difficulty in terms of military discipline, using them for military purposes, and also in terms of the way they behaved to citizens and the military organisation as such, in view of the discipline required.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Featherstone, I would suggest we make the break, please. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Mr. Karic, it's now time for the first break. During this break, please note that you should not discuss this evidence with anyone, and that includes members of the Prosecution who may be present at the location where the deposition is being taken. Thank you. We're adjourned now for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, Mr. Withopf. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karic, prior to the break you were describing the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades as being heavily involved in robberies against civilians and threats to kill civilians, and you were also emphasising the fact that such troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades were using drugs, resulting in further crimes. You were already touching on the issue of the military discipline. Such behaviour of the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades, what was the result in terms of military discipline, in terms of obeying to orders, and in terms of controlling the troops and their commanders, meaning Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat this second part of your question, because I did not hear it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The question was: To what extent the behaviour you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. describing in great detail prior to the break, to what extent did it result in problems in terms of military discipline, in terms of controlling the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades, and also in terms of control and/or command of the respective commanders, namely, Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. These manifestations on the part of these units and the members of these units were present. We in the main staff and in the General Staff were aware of them, and so was the Supreme Command, as a whole. However, the conditions were not right yet for taking some radical measures, as was the case in October 1993. We all thought that this was still a period when the military organisation was not mature enough yet, so to speak, and that as time went by, things would get in order, there would be appropriate discipline, and these units would be brought into the military organisation as a whole. So the General Staff did not actually deal with these issues, believing what I had already referred to. However, after Grabovica, and in view of the overall situation that was there, there was the decision taken by the General Staff and the Supreme Command to deal with these units in a military way, and that was done in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, the lack of military discipline, can you give us some concrete examples, examples that refer to the time period prior to the crime in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I myself know that it was often said that when they would be called by the commander of the 1st Corps of Sarajevo, Hajrulahovic Mustafa, Talijan that was the commander of that corps, that they would not respond when they were asked to come to the corps command to report. These two men who were within the military organisation differed from everybody else who behaved in a correct -- everybody else behaved in a correct fashion. There was behaviour that did not go along with military rules, such as the attack on the General Staff that was headquartered at the SDK building, and this preceded the events that took place in September 1993. They quite simply attacked some of the administrations that were in the SDK building, near the eternal flame. They wanted to deal with part of the General Staff in a military way, to settle accounts with them. Who knows what their intentions were, whether they wanted to carry out a coup d'etat, to take over power in the state. Who knows? This is behaviour that does not belong to the system itself. This is non-military behaviour and it is a reflection of a lack of discipline and willfulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, this coup d'etat, or attempted coup d'etat, just for clarification, did it happen prior to the crime in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I think that this was after the crime in Grabovica. I'd have to take a look. I'd have to take a look at my war diary in order to give a precise answer. So if you allow me to do so, I will. But I think this was towards the end of September 1993, after Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If you may please have a look, and the Prosecution will provide the Defence with a copy of that war diary. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Mr. Withopf, is there a copy available for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Such a copy will be made available after the next break. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Perhaps, Mr. Withopf, you could direct the witness to give us a page reference, so when he's referring to the diary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, once you've found the answer to the question, can you please indicate the page in the war diary you are referring to. PRESIDING OFFICER: I understand that we may have just the one copy here in The Hague. Would it be easier for everyone if it were placed on the ELMO so the interpreters and everyone can see it, and that would include, of course, Mr. Hodzic would be able to see it? Mr. Withopf, is it in English or in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It is in B/C/S. The copy Defence has been provided with is in B/C/S. PRESIDING OFFICER: I think that may be the -- Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's not possible to put it on the ELMO because that's the channel now for the videolink. So I'm sorry. I think maybe we can provide a copy to the interpreters later on, or as soon as possible. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Withopf, would it interrupt your chain of questioning very much to revert to this after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not at all. Not at all. PRESIDING OFFICER: And I think that may be the best way of proceeding so that copies can be available for everyone after the next break. So Mr. Karic, Mr. Withopf will take you to a new area of questioning, but we will return to this later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you were stating that -- now I'm quoting you: "We in the Main Staff were aware of such behaviour, as was the Supreme Command." Such behaviour is referring to the criminal conduct of the 9th and 10th Brigade and the fact that they were not under military control. Was Sefer Halilovic a member of the persons, of the bodies you were mentioning, the Main Staff and the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In terms of the position he held, he was a member of the Supreme Command, and of course, as chief of the Main Staff, he was the chief person in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Mr. Karic, that Mr. Halilovic, the accused, knew about the criminal behaviour you were just describing in great detail, criminal behaviour of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I assume that probably he knew quite a lot about that behaviour, but I also assume that the commanders themselves could have been with those smaller units and that this would change the attitude towards these units in terms of the lack of confidence that existed, precisely because of the brigade commanders. And Celo and Caco, commanders of the 9th and 10th Brigades, did bring these units of theirs into Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying that the accused, Sefer Halilovic, knew probably quite a lot about the criminal behaviour of such troops. On what facts is your assumption based upon?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I base it on the fact that we were often present in the Main Staff, where he was reported to as the chief of staff, and where these reports from various corps came in, according to the command and control principle. This came to his staff and to him personally. So I'm sure that he knew about quite a few things, that they were not in line with proper military organisation, and that various things were going on that should not happen in regular military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you are now saying you are sure that he knew about such behaviour because of the reports that have been discussed in the relevant body Mr. Halilovic has been a member of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps he did not know about every detail. Later on we learned a lot when these units were actually dealt with, when accounts were settled. But I'm sure that he knew that the behaviour of the commanders and the members of these units was not appropriate, in terms of military organisation and military establishment, and that it deviated from the other units in terms of their actual behaviour. The other units from the 1st Corps that were defending the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When did the accused, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, got to know --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: This has been discontinued.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. When, according to your knowledge, did Mr. Halilovic get to know about the criminal behaviour of the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: It is not one single step. It's not that he found out about this in one single day. This was ongoing behaviour that we all became aware of through reports that were coming in about negative things that were happening in units, in terms of arrogant behaviour, breaking into various facilities, say private property in Sarajevo, and so on and so forth. So Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this does not have to do with one particular date or one particular piece of information. This was present all the time, through the system of command and control, information was coming in about the conduct of all behaviors -- conduct of all units, about their behaviour, about their morale, about their sense of responsibility, discipline, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That I understand. Did he get to know prior to the crime in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, as you know, the crime in Grabovica was committed in September 1993, and that unit had existed since April 1992. So all of us were aware of a great many things, namely, that these two units, the 9th and the 10th, were not in line with the system of command and control, because of their behaviour, because of the criminal behaviour of certain groups of fighters from those units, because of the presence of drug addicts in these units, and their commanders were tolerating all of that. And also we believed that in due time this would be taken care of. This went all the way up to Grabovica, when they committed the crime they committed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: So the answer to my question would be Mr. Halilovic knew prior to the crime, of the criminal conduct of the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I would like to confirm this once again, in the following way: All of us in the Main Staff, including Mr. Sefer Halilovic, saw clearly that these units were not within the system of military control and command, military discipline, subordination, et cetera, and he did not expect, just like we didn't, that because of this knowledge of ours, through the information that we received about these units, that this would be exhibited in having this task carried out, or rather, that this would manifest itself in the form that they resorted to eventually. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Taking into account, Mr. Karic, that the criminal conduct of the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades was known to the direct superiors of such troops, but also to the superiors, including the Supreme Command staff of the ABiH, hasn't there been any attempt to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, probably because there wasn't enough time to deal with certain weaknesses in a radical fashion, in terms of replacing commanders, in terms of streamlining the troops. Because every day events in Sarajevo, and our overall engagement, made us postpone this until some later date. We were hoping that the time factor would contribute to having these units properly organised and that the day would come when they would be within a proper military chain of command and subordination. Quite simply, because of the gravity of the situation that we were all dealing with, we could not simply cut them off, and we could not say: As of tomorrow we're going to deal with the situation in the 9th Brigade and as of the day after tomorrow we are going to deal with the situation in the 10th Brigade. We're going to replace the commanders, et cetera. Because this would have been a major disservice in terms of the situation we had to deal with. We were defending the city and we were defending the lives of citizens in Sarajevo and in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When finally did the military leadership take action?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: The situation definitely became right in October 1993, when the command issued an order to the commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic, to deal with them in a military way. That is to say, to deal with the willfulness of the commanders of the 9th and 10th Brigades and to clear up the situation in those units. This is indeed what ensued in October 1993, and the results of this successful action are well known in terms of putting things into order. Later on, this yielded positive results.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Such a military action, was it discussed in the relevant bodies prior to October 1993, when the action actually took place, and was it discussed prior to the crime in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Prior to --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: People thought that this lack of discipline and wilful behaviour would be overcome within the foreseeable future, but then the crime was committed in Grabovica. They attempted to attack part of the Main Staff, and that was the straw that broke the camel's back. A decision was passed, and actually carried out in October 1993, when an order was issued by the Supreme Command of the presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina to deal with this in a military manner, and that was indeed done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Coming back, Mr. Karic, to the command -- 9th and 10th Brigades, Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic, what was the relation between the accused, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and such two commanders?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Sefer was in contact with Ramiz Delalic, the commander of the 9th Brigade, more frequently than with Musan Topalovic, but these relationships were -- the relations between us from the Main Staff and those two men, through Sefer, were the most successful, was the most successful type of contact. They respected Sefer Halilovic as the chief of staff, they obeyed his orders, and I think that all of us felt that Sefer, when dealing with these two units, had more personal authority, could exert more influence than the rest of us. At least, those were the conclusions I reached with regard to those relationships between Sefer Halilovic and the two commanders of the brigades we have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Karic, was there any particular reason why Sefer Halilovic had more influence on such troops as others?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, the commander of the 9th Brigade, is from Sandzak, and Sefer is from that place too. That's where he was born. So in a certain manner, the fact that they were both born in Sandzak culled their relationship, gave a certain tone to their relationship. Caco was from Sarajevo. It wasn't any easier with him than with other commanders who weren't from Sandzak. They didn't have these ties related to land, related to their origin, but the fact that the chief of the General Staff was in the Patriotic League, that he was a patriot, that he was an officer, and that he was in charge of the army right up until June 1993. This was normal for Caco too, and I think that he had more respect for Sefer's orders than for the orders of the commander of the 1st Corps, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Talijan. When Sefer ordered him to do something, he paid more attention to this than when his commander, the commander of the 1st Corps, ordered him to do something. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, are you happy to continue at the moment, or would you like to take a short break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would like to continue, I'm quite prepared to do so. I'm quite prepared to continue, but if you would like to have a break, I'll accept that too. PRESIDING OFFICER: I think we'll take just a five-minute break. It would be good. Thank you very much. Adjourned for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.19 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Please continue, Mr. Withopf. And Mr. Karic, if you do feel that you would like to take a break at any stage, please just do say so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, prior to the break, you were making reference to the good relationship between Sefer Halilovic and Ramiz Delalic. Despite this good relationship, was Sefer Halilovic not in a position to solve the problems with the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, given the passage of time, from this point of view, Sefer and all of us thought that a time would come when these issues would be solved, but the events in Grabovica and the attack against the operations centre of the General Staff brought things to a head and a decision was taken to deal with them in a military manner. We decided that we could no longer wait and tolerate such a situation and such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does it mean that prior to the crime in Grabovica, the Supreme Command, including Sefer Halilovic, just let things go, without taking any action? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: My answer would be as follows: We received quite a lot of information about this behaviour, which was not military, through investigations which were launched after combat, when many were arrested, and the -- we found out a lot of things in the course of that investigation, when, towards the end of 1993 and at the beginning of 1994, some men were arrested and ended up in prison. Many facts were not available to us, as to the -- as to how widespread their criminal behaviour was, although we knew that commanders were behaving in an undisciplined manner, and it depended on the mood they were in, whether they would turn up at a meeting depended on their mood if they were called to a meeting by the man called Talijan. So they were not behaving in a military manner. They weren't part of the military system. But they nevertheless carried out their main task, which was to protect the defence line that they had been assigned as a responsibility. No objections were made with regard to this issue. They carried out their basic tasks with regard to defending the town. If this had not been the case, it's quite certain that more severe steps would have been taken. But in the course of a number of specific events, given their violent behaviour with regard to citizens, their looting, we found out about this through the statements, towards the end of 1993 and at the beginning of 1994, the military court in Sarajevo obtained such information. So it was only then that we were fully informed about the real situation in those units, the situation that had preceded. But given the situation we were in, there was not that much that we could find out, and it was only at a quite late date that we did obtain information about these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the main task of the 9th and the 10th Brigade in defending the town? I assume you are referring to the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the city of Sarajevo, which is where they had the zone of responsibility and the defence position at the foot of Mount Trebevic, in the direction of the Jewish cemetery. That is where the line of defence of Caco's 10th Brigade was located, and the sharp stone feature, the north-western part of the defence of Sarajevo, above Sedrenik, that was the zone of responsibility of the 9th Brigade, under Ramiz Delalic, Celo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What has been the significance of the 9th and 10th Brigades, the significance in terms of defending certain areas of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: It was very significant, I would say. They had a very serious, an important task, because those areas were areas for the defence of Sarajevo. And there was ongoing combat at those lines. On the other side, in the immediate vicinity, the aggressor had his lines. That's where the aggressor's lines were, the lines from which they attacked the city of Sarajevo. And I'm referring to the forces of Republika Srpska. And it had the importance of the other brigades that were defending Sarajevo. Each brigade had its zone of responsibility, a designated area, and was responsible for that zone of responsibility. They had to defend the line and prevent the town from being threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Taking into account the importance of the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades in defending Sarajevo, what has been the reason why these troops have been sent to participate in Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: The main reason is that these units had been brought up to strength, as per establishment. Their zones of responsibility were not as long as the other units that were defending Sarajevo. So it was easier to take some of the men from those brigades, because this would not pose threat to the defence of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You are saying it was the easiest to take some of the men of such two military units. What's the number we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: The most rational, not the east easiest. It would not have resulted in weakening the units that were defending Sarajevo. They had been brought up to strength, as per establishment, and their zone of responsibility was not that large. This is what Vahid Karavelic, the commander at the time, suggested at the time, at the meeting with Rasim Delic, the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how many fighters were finally brought to Herzegovina of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Together with the Independent Battalion of Adnan Solakovic, there were about 300 fighters in total I think that about 210 combatants, one from the 9th -- from those two brigades. I think about 210 to 215 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how many of them were from the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, about the same number, from the 9th and 10th, between 105 and 110 combatants from both brigades. That would be a total of between 210 and 220. The other men up to 300, were from the Independent Battalion of Adnan Solakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who made the decision to select the 9th and the 10th Brigades to participate in Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Who took the decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: The decision was taken at a meeting with the commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who was present at --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: We were all present from the Main Staff, the chiefs of various branches, Sefer Halilovic, as the chief of the Main Staff, and the Corps Commander, the commander of the 1st Corps, Vahid Karavelic, the commander of the 1st Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For verification, do I understand you correctly that Sefer Halilovic was present when the decision has been made to have the 9th and 10th Brigades participating in Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He attended the meeting at which we discussed, for a long period of time, which units it would be easiest to use in the NERETVA-93 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sefer Halilovic raise any objections against using troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades for Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he didn't, nor did any of the others who were present at that meeting. What was important was to take some of the forces from the 1st Corps and to ensure that in so doing we would not be placing the defence of Sarajevo at risk. No one was wondering how those people would behave. That meeting was a lengthy one. We analysed in detail the various issues and we were satisfied that we would be in a position to maintain the defence of Sarajevo but that we would nevertheless have forces, the strength of one battalion, and this was essential for us, forces from these two brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When did the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades, after the decision has been made, when did they arrive in the area, in the area of Operation NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: There were some complications with regard to their departure. Sefer returned to Sarajevo. He tried to hurry things up. The reason was the weather, a storm, the lack of fuel for a vehicle for his transport, et cetera. But I think that they arrived -- well, just a minute. Let me find the exact date. We arrived -- Caco and Ramiz Delalic arrived from Sarajevo with their men on the 6th of September, 1993. That's what it states in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly, Mr. Karic, that there was some delay with the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades arriving in the area and Mr. Halilovic went back to Sarajevo to take care of it?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Where did the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigade actually arrive?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm consulting my war diary to find the date. That was the 6th of 9, 1993. Caco and Delalic, Ramiz, came from Sarajevo, their men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where had you set up your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: In Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the troops arrived in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, going back to Sarajevo to speed up the arrival of the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades, and also of the 2nd Independent Battalion, wasn't it very difficult at the time to go from Jablanica to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that it was --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: One would have to go almost up to Konjic by vehicle from Celebici, along the railroad, above the Jablanica lake that was exposed to HVO fire. So then this would have to take place only during the night, and then over the hills above Konjic, and finally one would arrive in Konjic. From Konjic to Pazarici, one would have to take the M17 road and then across Mount Igman. One would have to drive during the night, without any lights on, and there was enemy fire there along that road day and night. So it was very difficult to reach Hrasnica. And then one would have to go through the well-known tunnel underneath the airport. It was 800 metres long. And that's how one would get into Sarajevo. So this involved a great deal of psychological and physical stress. So it was quite a feat to reach Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Why did Mr. Sefer Halilovic, why did he make such efforts you are just describing as physical stress, why did he make such efforts to go to Sarajevo to speed up the arrival of the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Those units were supposed to go out between the 1st and 2nd of September, 1993. Because of the bad weather on one particular day - I think it was between the 3rd and 4th - we received information from the commander of the 1st Corps, Vahid Karavelic, that the units could not leave because of the bad weather, because of the heavy rainfall. And vehicles did not have enough fuel for getting from Hrasnica. Sefer, with the best of intentions, wanting to carry out the orders of the head of the Main Staff, and he wanted the preparations for this operation to be in line with the order, and he saw that there were certain obstructions in terms of the arrival of units, and also some of the materiel that these units were supposed to bring along, decided to take this step. He wanted to resolve the problem by way of his own presence, and he wanted the units to get out of Sarajevo. I think that that was the main reason. He realised that through radio communications that were very difficult anyway, he could not make sure that this order would be carried out and that these units would arrive as planned. That's why he decided to go to Sarajevo and to use his own influence and authority to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were detailing two reasons, Mr. Karic, why Mr. Sefer Halilovic went to Sarajevo and why there was a delay in the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades arriving in Jablanica. The first reason has been heavy rainfall, and the second reason, there was not sufficient fuel. Heavy rainfall is certainly not a reason Mr. Sefer Halilovic could influence at the time, and in your opinion, was it necessary for Sefer Halilovic, in his very high position, to go to Sarajevo to sort out the issue about the lack of fuel?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I would like to say that this was necessary, for the following reasons: In the situation that we were in, we, the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the time that we are talking about, the logistics and the military organisation were not in a position to have certain things carried out, and maintain military subordination and a proper attitude towards orders. I think it was crucial, the fact that Sefer went there to talk to Caco. Once again, I think he did this in Hrasnica. There was some wavering in terms of having this order carried out. Also, through the commander of the 4th Brigade, stationed in Hrasnica, again through his personal influence, he made sure that a few vehicles were found, as well as fuel, and then these units had set out. Had Sefer not gone to Sarajevo, I'm sure that until the present day, these units would not have arrived and taken part in that task. Because any kind of pretext was sought not to go to Herzegovina. And who knows what was in the heads of -- he was supposed to return his men from Hrasnica. He was not supposed to go, in spite of the orders of the corps command and of the Main Staff, and so on and so forth. This is the situation that we lived in, and this is what the times were like.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that there was a discontinuation between two parts of the statement. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Withopf, is that a convenient moment or would you like to just clarify that break in the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify one particular issue. PRESIDING OFFICER: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At that time, where has been Rasim Delic and where has been Vahid Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: At that time, they were in Sarajevo, in their respective commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Where Rasim Delic, as the commander of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Vahid Karavelic, as the commander of the 1st Corps, would they be able to order the troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades to move to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: They were in a position to give orders, and they did so. However, their attitude, especially that of Musan Topalovic, Caco, was unpredictable, and he stopped the unit in Hrasnica when he passed through the tunnel and they got some rest during that night, and quite simply, he himself came to the conclusion that he was not supposed to carry out this order; rather, that when night fell, he should return his unit to Sarajevo. He didn't feel like going to Herzegovina. That is how some of their minds worked, because the military organisation was insufficient, immature, in relation to some other normal armies in Europe and worldwide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying, Mr. Karic, that each and every pretext was used to not move to Herzegovina. Are you referring to the heavy --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As far as Caco was concerned, yes. He was quite persistent. And later on I found out that Sefer had talked to him in Hrasnica, and he barely managed to convince him that he should leave for Jablanica on that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: So there was a decision of the Supreme Command that troops and the commanders of the 9th and 10th Brigades didn't obey to and they only obeyed to Mr. Sefer Halilovic? Is that a correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not the way I'd put it. Quite simply, they obeyed orders, and they left Sarajevo, although they delayed it for a day or two because of bad weather. Nevertheless, the weather can never be a factor for the military not to carry out an order. But in that situation, that's the way it was. When they got out of Sarajevo through that tunnel, when they got to Hrasnica, then Caco simply changed the decision, and had Sefer not been there and had he not talked to him and exercised his own influence and authority, I believe that no one else could have persuaded Caco to go and carry out the task, the assignment. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: So Mr. Sefer Halilovic finally ordered Caco, Musan Topalovic, to move to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We would suggest to make a break of 15 minutes. PRESIDING OFFICER: Indeed. We'll adjourn for 15 minutes and then resume for the full hour, so that we get the best possible sitting time in today. Thank you. We're adjourned for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: We'll wait for Mr. Withopf. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes. Is he on his way?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was up to collect the copies. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So he should be back here. PRESIDING OFFICER: And I see we don't have the witness either in the seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: It's working very well for the technical arrangement. PRESIDING OFFICER: Well, I think I'll withdraw, and when Mr. Withopf and the witness are here, we'll resume. We needn't worry too much about the formalities. --- Break taken at 12.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Withopf, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We are ready to continue, and Ms. Tuma will continue. PRESIDING OFFICER: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karic. My name is Marie Tuma and I am the one who is representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the speaker, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So I will now continue with the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And now we're moving on to another area, and that is about the accommodation of the soldiers. Mr. Karic, you said earlier that the soldiers from the 9th and 10th Brigade, as well as the Independent Battalion, arrived in the area on the 6th September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was there any arrangement done for their accommodation of the soldiers, and who was then in charge of this accommodation of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to start again because we didn't hear the beginning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: At the meeting of the power supply company, of course we thought about where these people should be accommodated once they had arrived, because in Jablanica there were about 10.000 refugees from Prozor and from other areas that had already been occupied by the HVO. So in Jablanica, there was no other accommodation. There could have been no other accommodation, precisely because the refugees had arrived in Jablanica previously and were therefore staying at all the facilities that were available. However, we ordered Zulfikar-Zuko Alispago because he was the local commander in Donja Jablanica together with his units and his area of responsibility was Grabovica as well, that he should be responsible for the accommodation of the incoming troops from Sarajevo, and that's exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When was this meeting --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: He, together with his men, took the troops in and provided accommodation for them. During the preparations, a few days before that, I can tell you exactly. This was on the 2nd of September, 1993. At this provisional command post in Jablanica, where the commanders of local units, the 44th and the 45th units were called to, also the unit of Zulfikar-Zuko Alispago and some other people from the municipal staff of Territorial Defence, where assignments were given, those that specifically had to do with accommodation. Zuka was given that particular order and he did carry it out, in terms of receiving the troops and putting them up in Donja Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And was this concerning both the 9th and 10th and the Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. All units that came from Sarajevo, except that Zuka decided that somewhere in the area of Donja Jablanica, by the transformer station, he found some facilities for putting up part of the men from the 10th Brigade, about half of them, and all the rest were put up in Donja Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Where is Donja Grabovica located?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: On the M17 road, in the direction of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And why --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Somewhere halfway between Jablanica, Dreznica, there is a hydroelectric power plant of Grabovica in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And why was then Grabovica selected as a spot to accommodate those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, we were in such a situation that we did not have the necessary logistics that other armies have, normal armies, so that the army can stay in proper camps, under tents, et cetera. It so happened that we never had any of this, throughout the war. So for the most part, we had to stay with the local population, wherever there was room, along with previous coordination and contacts with the population. For a certain amount of time, they would take soldiers in, at least part of the soldiers in, and put them up in barns, sheds, et cetera, because that was the only possibility available. We knew that these units would be used in combat in the area of the hills, and Grabovica was the closest in that area, and Jablanica was oversaturated. There was simply nowhere to stay in Jablanica, because as I already mentioned, 10.000 refugees from Herzegovina had arrived in Jablanica over the preceding months. So all of that is the way it was in terms of using the troops, and then also on the left bank of the Neretva River were the Igman Wolves, the unit of Zuka. And also the HVO in Herceg-Bosna had just released some camp inmates and we put them up in some of the prefabricated buildings that were there, so we gave them whatever we could by way of assistance. On the right bank of the Neretva River, in about ten houses, it was mostly elderly Croats who lived there, old men, for the most part --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: And they had enough room --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Enough room to take people in.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So if we go back a bit here, the 9th Brigade, were they then accommodated in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And 10th Brigade, where was this brigade accommodated?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I said a short while ago, approximately half of that brigade was in Grabovica, and the rest were in the northern part of Jablanica, near the transformer station in Gornja Jablanica. Solakovic's battalion was over there in Grabovica too.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And how many soldiers was it in total that were located in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Approximately about 200 or 210 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you visit, Mr. Karic, the village before this was arranged?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you then describe the village for us, please. How many people were living there, about, and in how many houses, if there were civilians, and their age, and so on, please.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of days before the units were Sarajevo arrived, we visited the inhabitants of the village of Grabovica. Rifat Bilajac, Zicro Suljevic, and Iso Alic were with me. We visited all the houses and spoke to the people. They were mainly elderly Croats who hadn't moved anywhere. They were living there peacefully. When we asked them whether they had enough room in their houses and on the grounds of the houses, as it was still warm and it was also possible to use stalls, we asked them whether they could take in soldiers arriving from Sarajevo for a few days. No one objected to this. They all agreed. There were between 10 and 15 houses, and in each house there was one elderly member of the household, with his wife, with the exception of one house, in which an old woman and a young woman lived, and another house, there was a girl of about 25 years, and her mother. The other people were all elderly and no one objected to our request for them to take combatants in. We had no other solution. We wanted them to be billeted there. We said that they would be safe and that no one would pose a risk to them. They agreed and we returned to our command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So the village was inhabited by normal civilians, elderly people, men and women. Were there any children as well?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: There were some children, but not many. There were some children in two houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, did you or someone else report about this accommodation of the soldiers of the 9th and the 10th Brigades to Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
