utterances.text: Well, when he returned from Sarajevo, Sefer was informed of the arrival of the units and of the fact that we had found accommodation for them. We discussed this matter at the command post, when Sefer returned to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When was --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: So he knew where they had been billeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When was Sefer Halilovic informed about the accommodation of the units? You said that it was when he arrived in Sarajevo. Can you remember when this was, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I think it was when Sefer returned from Sarajevo on the 7th, the 7th of September, 1993. It was at that point that Sefer was informed of all the issues. He was informed of what we had done during his absence, and he was also informed about the units that had arrived from Sarajevo, about the accommodation that had been found for them, et cetera. PRESIDING OFFICER: Ms. Tuma, before you continue, I notice that the witness is referring to the diary and using it to remind himself of various dates. I think it would perhaps be appropriate for it to now be presented, and at least marked for identification, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For identification, we will use this diary, and we now have the necessary copies available. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked for identification, ID P1.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you said here just recently that Sefer Halilovic was informed about the accommodation of the soldiers, and what was he informed about more exactly?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: As I said, Sefer was absent for a few days, when he went to Sarajevo. And when returning, and returning was not that easy, it was necessary to pass over Mount Igman, get as far as Jablanica, over the bridge, in Celebici, which was directly exposed to HVO fire. We informed him of everything we had done during his absence, and we informed him of the arrival of the units from Sarajevo and of the fact that they had been billeted. We also informed him of all other matters that he needed to be informed about. We told him about the problems we had with logistics, what we had managed to achieve so far, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was Sefer Halilovic informed that the soldiers were accommodated in a Croatian village inhabited by Croatian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether Sefer knew that Croats lived there, but I assume that he did at that time. Whether they were Bosniaks or Croats was not important to us. These people were elderly people who had lived in that area before the war and were still living in that area at that time. No one posed a threat to them. In fact, Zulfikar Alispago's units protected them, secured transport to the clinic for them, assisted them in various ways by providing food and in other ways. It was not at all a matter of whether they were Bosniaks or Croats. These were elderly people who had agreed to help. So we didn't give any importance to this matter. It wasn't something that occupied us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Karic --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Preoccupied us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, was Sefer Halilovic then informed that this village was inhabited by elderly civilians?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say so, given the time that has passed, I couldn't say anything about this matter, since there were far more important issues. This was not an issue for the command, of which we were a part at the time. We were not in a position to anticipate what was going to happen in order to be able to take more radical action. I'm not at all sure that Sefer was aware of the fact that the people living there were elderly Croats. I don't know whether we informed him about this too. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You said here recently, Mr. Karic, that you assumed that Sefer Halilovic did know that there were civilians living in this village. By what means do you assume that?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Later he probably found out through Zulfikar Alispago that it was a Croatian village near the Dreznica station and that elderly people, Croats, lived there, on the whole, with some children. They were living in these 15 to 20 houses, up to two or three people in each household, in each house. So Sefer was not in a position to personally verify this. So I don't think that Sefer was aware of those details during the period that we are referring to, because it was not necessary to inform about this. We had other matters to deal with. It was not necessary to go into these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, by your knowledge, did Mr. Sefer Halilovic visit the area of Grabovica prior to the crime that occurred later on?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: We were reconnoitring during those days, in one of the hills to the east of the M17 road, below Grabovica, and when returning, we went to the barracks in -- to the hut in Grabovica, where Zuka's -- Igman Wolves were from and we spoke to the detainees there. But we didn't cross the bridge, the little bridge over the Neretva River, in order to enter Grabovica. We didn't have the time to do so, and nor was it necessary to do so. To what extent Sefer was able to know that there were houses there by the station, I don't know, but Zulfikar's units were on the left bank of the Neretva River and above the road there were about a hundred detainees who had been released from the HVO camp in Herceg-Bosna. These people were Bosniaks. We spoke to them, examined them, called doctors, organised the provision of food for them, and organised their lives in those huts.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, when was this? You have remembered that?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, was this in September?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in September.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And in the beginning of September?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: For the event in Grabovica. At the beginning of September. I won't look for it in the war diary, but I have the exact date. Before the unfortunate events in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Karic, despite the fact that we heard earlier on today that the 9th and 10th Brigade was sort of well known for criminal behaviour before the arrival in Grabovica, was it then a good idea to locate and accommodate those units in this village inhabited by civilians?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Whether it was a good idea?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC
utterances.text: Those units in Sarajevo, if I may, I'll explain this - they weren't involved. They didn't display the syndrome of the HVO aggression, a former ally, freje [phoen], when on the 25th of October they attacked Prozor and turned their backs on us, and our former friends became our enemy. This was not felt -- this aspect, the common fight against the aggressor, was present in Sarajevo. It had not been disrupted, regardless of the fact that for one year in Herzegovina this relationship was quite different. This wasn't present among us, because these people had not been infected by such an inimical attitude, especially not towards elderly people and especially not towards people who were putting them up and providing them with food, et cetera. It's another matter to say that we did not have the possibility of finding accommodation in camps for men arriving from Sarajevo, and to avoid them coming into contact with civilians, Bosniaks or Croats. It was not objectively possible for us, and given the situation, we did not even think about this very much. What was important for us was to find accommodation for these men they had to rest from the trip from Sarajevo and they had to prepare for the combat action for which they had been brought there. That is how we viewed the matter at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm done, Mr. Karic, so thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Featherstone, the Prosecution anticipates the cross-examination completely be finished within 30 to 35 minutes, so if we could continue today, it would certainly be a good decision to do so. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, I think that would be useful. So you did say the cross-examination. You mean, your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Direct examination. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes. I think it would be excellent, as long as there's no objection from the interpreters or the technical staff. That would mean we would continue until about half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. PRESIDING OFFICER: That's fine? Thank you. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, there are only a few issues we wish to continue to address in the examination-in-chief today, and the first issue relates to sending troops of the 9th and 10th Brigades from Sarajevo to Jablanica. In that respect, the Prosecution wishes to tender into evidence two documents, VK1 and VK2, and I will read out the documents to you, the contents of the documents to you, since I understand it cannot be done in any electronic way. PRESIDING OFFICER: Subject to anything the registrar has to say about that, I think you're correct, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can check. One second, please. PRESIDING OFFICER: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apparently the documents are available in Sarajevo, so they can electronically show them on the ELMO, with the camera in Sarajevo. Or -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There are documents available in Sarajevo, but not the ones we wish to address.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then it's not possible. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. Then I'm afraid you will have to read them out, Mr. Withopf. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The documents are short ones. Therefore, it will not be any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, the first document I wish to read out to you concerns the order of the accused Mr. Sefer Halilovic to bring troops from the 9th and 10th Brigades from Sarajevo to Jablanica. The document is dated -- the order is dated the 2nd of September, 1993. It's signed by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, as the deputy commander and chief of the General Staff, and it reads as follows, and now I'm quoting the contents of the document: "HVO and HV are using Muslims as live shields and are conquering parts of the town. On a daily basis, they are shelling our population in the valley of Neretva. HVO proclaimed Mostar its capital and is taking all necessary measures to conquer it. To stop these intentions, I am ordering: "1. Brigade 'Delta', parts of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade and Colakovic's unit all equivalent 300 soldiers and more with complete equipment and arms prepare and send latest Friday night, 3rd of September, 1993, to Bradina where they will be accepted by the command of the 6th Corps. "2. If you believe that by this separation, the defence of Sarajevo is jeopardised, I am prepared to take full personal responsibility. "3. On realisation of this assignment under item 1 of this order, inform me through packet-radio of the command of the 6th Corps." That's the quote from the order of 2nd September 1993, and I'm also making reference to a second order -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Withopf, before you move on, could we just clarify: Is that the entire document that you've read?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's almost the entire document. There are information about to whom had has been forwarded. It has been forwarded to the command of the 1st Corps, to the command of GSS VK, expansion unknown, and commander of the 6th Corps, and it has been sent from the centre of communications Sarajevo, date and time 2nd of September, 1993, Thursday, at 11.14 hours, and it's dated the 2nd September of 1993. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Withopf, perhaps you could establish with the witness whether or not he's familiar with this document, and if there is to be some detailed questioning about it, I think perhaps we would need to make arrangements to get a copy to him in Sarajevo for tomorrow. I think it is only appropriate that the witness should be able to see the document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If the need arises. I have only a very few questions in relation to this document and in relation to the second one, which is even much shorter. If the need arises, we can make such documents available. PRESIDING OFFICER: Well, I think we may need to. If we can establish whether the witness is at least familiar with the document, that would help. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The second document, Mr. Karic, it's also dated the 2nd of September, 1993. It has the initials SH and VK. It's a document dated the 2nd September 1993, addressed to the ABiH 1st Corps command. The document is entitled "request regarding leaving of ABiH 1st Corps units," and it reads as follows: "Ask for urgent response regarding the order to ABiH --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: "ABiH 1st Corps units to leave for the valley of Neretva. The time of departure and number of soldiers were requested in order to organise shelter and transport."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Withopf, could you please repeat the reading of this passage. The French booth did not get it at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It reads as follows -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Withopf, I'm sorry. I'm going to interrupt you. The registry have some additional technical information. Apparently it is now possible to have this document displayed and perhaps the registrar would either explain the technicalities or actually implement them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It can be put on the ELMO now. They have changed the cameras, or something like that, in Sarajevo. So if you place it on the ELMO and they can show it to the witness. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, do you see a document before you yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. PRESIDING OFFICER: Sorry. Could you kindly repeat that, please, court deputy. We didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's much better now. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. We are literally in the dark at this end, so if there's any difficulty with the document, please inform us immediately and we'll do what we can. Thank you. Mr. Withopf, if you'd like to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is one problem with the clarity of the document. PRESIDING OFFICER: Is it legible?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It needs to be focused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It needs to be focused. PRESIDING OFFICER: I hope the technical booth is assisting us here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's acceptable now. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Then, Mr. Withopf, if you'd like to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, the document you have now in front of you, it's signed by Mr. Sefer Halilovic. It's dated the 2nd of September, 1993. And it orders that parts of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade and Colakovic unit should move to Bradina, where they will be accepted by the command of the 6th Corps. Can you read the document in B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We no longer see the document. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. We heard you there. It looks as though this is not actually going to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And I would suggest we transmit copies of the documents to Sarajevo and the witness will be shown the documents tomorrow morning. PRESIDING OFFICER: Indeed. I think that's most appropriate. Is there any line of questioning you'd like to continue with today, Mr. Withopf, or should we conclude for today and carry on tomorrow? We can perhaps stretch some extra time, if needed, but we seem to be doing quite well on the schedule at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We are actually doing very well on the schedule and I would suggest we continue tomorrow morning. We have very few questions in relation to these two documents and we -- to address another issue, we anticipate it will take us some 30 minutes. PRESIDING OFFICER: That's fine. Sarajevo, we can't actually see you but I assume you're hearing us. We will adjourn for the today and resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: 1.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of July 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
